## Part 2: Population Density

For the population density analysis, we will analyze data from Shaws Cove, Heisler Park, and Treasure Cove. Create a data frame that excludes the Corona del Mar data, as that site did not have area measured.

```{r}
No_CDM_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site != "Corona del Mar") #The != means not equal to, while == means equal to. 
No_CDM_Sizes
```

#### 2.1. How many limpets did we measure at each site in each year for sizes?

Use nrow(), group_by() and count() to tally the limpet observations at each transect. We used the same transect numbers at Shaws and Heisler, so group_by() site as well.

```{r}
No_CDM_Sizes

# How many did we measure total, across both sites?
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  nrow() #The nrow() function tells us the total number of rows within the dataset. We can use this to tell us the total number of limpets measured because each row is a single observation. 

## How many did we measure at each site? 
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(year, site) |> #The group_by() function groups/splits the date by the columns specified. For this example, the observations are grouped by year and site.
  count() #The count() function counts the unique number of rows within the dataset and excludes any row that has matching data across ALL columns. 
  

# How many did we measure in each transect? 
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(year, site, transect_num) |> 
  count()
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(year, site, transect_num, transect_length_m) |> 
  count() |> 
   mutate(density = n/(transect_length_m*2)) #The mutate() function allows for new cokumns to be added to the dataset. The name on the lef tof the equal sign is the new column name. The information on the right of the equal sign is what columns you are pulling dataframe and what you are doing to it to get new data. In this example, we are calculating density using transect length. 
  
  

Limpet_Density
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
Limpet_Density$density |> #The $ signifies that we only want to work within a particular column. On the left side is the dataset we are pulling from and on the right is the column we are pulling from. 
  mean() #The mean() function calculates the mean of the data inputed. 

Limpet_Density$density |> 
  sd() #The sd() function calculates the standard deviation of the data inputed.

n <- Limpet_Density$density |> #We must calculate the number of observations, n, of our dataset.
  length() #The length() function tells us how many elements, or observations, are in the dataset. 

Limpet_Density$density |> 
  sd()/sqrt(n) #This is the formula for calculating standard error.
```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |>
  group_by(year, site) |> 
  summarize( #The summarize() function creates the summary statistics that is requested of the dataset. In this example, we want the summary statistics for density and we calculate the mean, sd, se, and n.
    mean_density = mean(density), # mean 
            sd_density = sd(density),  # standard deviation
            n = n(), # count
            se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)) |>  # standard error
  mutate_at(vars(mean_density, sd_density, se_density), 
            .funs = round, 2) # This line reduces/rounds the data calculated in our summary statistics table. The vars() function distinguishes which variables we are going to change. 
  
  
  
  
 
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

-   Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? Yes it is continuous.

-   Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? Yes it is random.

-   Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? There is homogeneity of variance.

-   Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal? Yes, the distribution is approximately normal.

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

-   Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

-   Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

-   Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(year != "2024")
CDM_TC_Sizes
  
# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes) #The lm() function creates a linear model based off of the chosen variables within the dataset. The DV is on the left of the ~ and the IV is on the right. 
model

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1) #The plot() function creates a residuals vs fitted plot, and others, of the linear model we created above. The which = 1 portion says we only want to view the first plot created which is residuals vs fitted. 

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

-   Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2) #The QQ plot is the second plot produced by the plot() function and that is why which = 2.

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals) #The Shapiro-Wilk test tells us if the data is distributed normally. 
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes, var.equal = FALSE) #The var.equal = FALSE tells us that the variance is not equal and this must be taken into consdireation when running a t-test.
```

#### [3.4 - Interpret and explain the results of your test]{.underline}

Are we pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations? Why is the standard error so small?

We are confident that these samples were drawn from different populations because there is no overlap in errorbars and the result of our t-test shows that there is a significant difference in the mean shell length between limpets found at Corona del Mar and Treasure Cove (p-value \< 0.05). The standard error is so small because the data has low variability and the data is precise.

#### 4.1 Territory Data

Clean up and combine the 2023, 2024 and 2025 data for Territories:

```{r}
load(file = "Data/All_Territories.Rdata")

load(file = "Data/FenbergTerr.Rdata")

All_Territories

All_Territories |> 
  relocate(site, year, .before = location) |> 
  relocate(year, .before = site) #The relocate() function allows us to rearrange the columns into specific orders. The columns listed before the comma are the ones we are moving and after the comma designates where we are moving it to. 
```

#### 4.2 How many limpet territories did we measure?

```{r}
## How many territories were measured at each site in each year? 
All_Territories |> 
  select(site, year) |> 
  group_by(year, site) |> 
  mutate(count = n()) |> 
  distinct()
```

#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

-   territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

-   Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
  select(site, year, habitat, size_mm, numbsquares) |> 
  mutate(area_mm2 = numbsquares * 361) |> 
  mutate(mass_g = 0.00009*size_mm ^ 3.0471)
  # create a new column for territory area in mm^2 using the "numbsquares" column
         # mesh = 19 mm x 19 mm 
All_Territories_area_mass

  # create a new column for limpet body mass
  # formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471

```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(log(mass_g), log(area_mm2)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
log_model <- lm(log(area_mm2) ~ log(mass_g), data = All_Territories_area_mass)
  
plot(log_model, which = 1)
plot(log_model, which = 2)
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}

summary(log_model)

```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

#### 4.9 Compare the relationship we found to the original study.

```{r}
FenbergTerr

# Plot the Fenberg data with the log transformations
FenbergTerr |> 
  ggplot() +
  aes(log(mass_g), log(area_mm2)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
 

# Find the slope and intercept of the best fit line
Fenberg_model <- lm(log(area_mm2) ~ log(mass_g), data = FenbergTerr)

summary(Fenberg_model)


```

Explain your findings!

The slope of the line of best fit is 0.8916 and the intercept of the line of best fit is 7.91. This means the line of best fit equation for the Fenberg data is y = 0.8916x + 7.910. The line of best fit equation for the All_Territories data is y = 0.8903 + 8.2116. Comparing the best fit lines of the log transformed data shows that the Fenberg data follows the same patterns found in the All_Territories data where for every one additional mm2 of territory about 0.89 grams of mass are added to the owl limpet.
